cim: Georgia High School Students Weigh Learning Without Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Georgia High School Students Weigh Learning Without Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has become popularized for use in academics. So for some students, it's hard to imagine getting stuck on a homework question and not being able to turn to AI for a quick answer. For a number of scholars at Arabia Mountain High School, that's become part of their everyday routine. With teachers setting limits on when AI can be used, students are spending more time figuring things out on their own. Some say it's helping them learn, while others admit it's making schoolwork more challenging.

AI has become a popular tool for students who need help understanding assignments, brainstorming ideas, or finding answers. But how much help is too much? At Arabia Mountain High School, students have different opinions. Some believe AI makes learning easier, while others worry students are becoming too dependent on it.

Under DeKalb County School District (DCSD) guidelines, teachers decide when students can use AI for assignments. Students must follow those directions and cannot turn in AI-generated work as their own without permission. The challenge, according to Robert Calloway, a teacher at Arabia Mountain High School, is finding a balance between using technology and making sure students are actually learning.

For some students, working without AI hasn't changed much. For others, it means spending more time on assignments and finding different ways to get help.

Gabrielle Montgomery, a senior at Arabia Mountain High School, said she doesn't normally use AI for schoolwork, so the restrictions haven't really affected her. Still, she understands why some students might struggle without it.

“Some assignments take much longer when I’m stuck trying to answer something on my own,” Montgomery said.

Even though working independently can be frustrating, Montgomery believes it has its benefits.

“It can force you to actually learn the material instead of depending on something else to give you the answers,” she said.

Melissa Mendoza, a senior at Arabia Mountain High school, has noticed a bigger difference in how she approaches schoolwork. She used to rely on AI to help brainstorm ideas and find answers, but now she's learning to work through assignments herself.

“My critical thinking skills have become sharper, and I actually exercise my abilities,” Mendoza said.

She admitted that when she used AI more often, she wasn't always paying attention during class. Instead of listening to the lesson, she sometimes looked up assignments online and used AI to help complete them.

Now, she says she's more focused and confident in her ability to answer questions.

“I’m actually taking in the information rather than finding a quick answer and jotting it down,” she said.

But there's a downside. According to Mendoza, completing assignments on her own takes more time, which sometimes means less time to hang out with friends. Still, even with the extra work, she said finishing an assignment by herself “feels like a reward.”

Mariam Dukuray, a senior at Arabia Mountain High School, has taken a different approach. When she doesn't understand something, she often turns to Khan Academy or YouTube for help.

“Unlike AI, it might take a while to find a video that explains exactly what I’m confused about,” Dukuray said. “However, those videos are still teaching me step by step, so I’m actually learning the material.”

She understands why students like using AI, especially when they need an answer quickly. But she also worries about what happens when students start depending on it for everything.

Another concern is that students may miss important learning opportunities when they rely too much on AI. Although AI can provide quick answers, students still need to practice solving problems and thinking critically on their own. Finding a balance between using AI as a helpful resource and completing work independently can help students understand the material better.

“If I use AI every time I don’t know an answer, I might not give myself enough time to think or try to solve it on my own,” she said.

Dukuray also believes there's something important about getting help from another person.

“Sometimes talking to an actual person helps me understand something better,” she said.

Although the students have different experiences, they agree that AI doesn't have to be completely removed from education.

Gabrielle Montgomery believes there should be a difference between using AI to do an assignment and using it to help understand a difficult topic or prepare for a test.

Melissa Mendoza thinks AI could be useful for creative group projects and for explaining information in ways students can better understand.

Mariam Dukuray also believes teachers should think about how they use AI. She said students may feel less motivated to put effort into their assignments when they notice teachers relying heavily on AI to create classroom materials.

Their opinions show that the conversation isn't just about whether students should use AI. It's also about how schools can make sure the technology is helping students learn instead of doing the learning for them.

DeKalb County School District has guidelines explaining how AI can be used in schools. Teachers decide whether students can use AI based on the assignment and what they're expected to learn.

Students must follow their teachers' instructions and cannot submit AI-generated work as their own unless they have permission. Using AI without authorization can be considered an academic integrity violation and may lead to consequences under the district's Student Code of Conduct.

The guidelines also address inappropriate uses of AI, including creating deepfakes, impersonating others, harassment, and using AI for unauthorized help on tests.

At the same time, the district recognizes that students need to understand how to use AI responsibly. DCSD's Instructional Technology website highlights its Gemini AI Certification Program, which introduces students to topics such as AI safety, digital citizenship, writing effective prompts, and using AI in real-world situations.

As AI continues to become part of everyday life, schools will have to figure out how to prepare students to use the technology while still encouraging them to think independently.

AI might be able to give students like Montgomery, Mendoza, and Dukuray an answer in seconds, but knowing the answer isn't always the same as understanding it. For these Arabia Mountain High School students, learning when to use AI and when to figure things out on their own may be one of the most important lessons of all.

This article was written by Sofia Robertson, a student reporter in Robert Calloway's A/V and Film class at Arabia Mountain High School in Stonecrest, Georgia.
